query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

Despite our recent observations of various toughening mechanisms occurring on the nanometre length-scale in the vicinity of a crack tip in such an alloy, the quantitative strengthening effect from deformation twinning and the nature of twinning-induced plasticity remain somewhat uncertain. Simultaneous increase in strength and ease of plastic deformation (or ductility) is the ultimate goal for most structural materials, but is usually mutually exclusive. A new class of metallic alloys, known as high-entropy alloys (HEA), have shown great promise in overcoming this conflict. HEAs are comprised of multiple metallic elements—usually five or more—in equal or near equal concentrations that crystallize as single-phase solid solutions with simple crystal structures,. In particular, one of the most-studied HEA systems to show the coveted combination of strength and ductility is the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi with a single-phase fcc structure,. Later studies of various derivatives of this alloy showed that the ternary CrCoNi—also crystallizing in a single fcc phase—exhibits even higher cryogenic strength, ductility and fracture toughness, making it superior to its quinary parent HEA or any of its other equiatomic fcc ternary or quaternary derivatives,. Despite current interest in CrCoNi, the exact origin of its excellent mechanical properties still remains unclear.
